<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# Improve the staged experiment

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a snapshot you may repair: inspect its
source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic,
logs, tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation evidence. Do not assume that an
unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed
behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health.

## Your job

If you find a defect, fix it in the staged workspace at `/workspace`. **Do not
launch training.** Do not start the experiment, in the foreground or
background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
anything you launch is wasted and scores nothing. Cheap, non-training checks
are fine. **Do not use the network.** Do not fetch code, documentation,
packages, or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose
and repair using only what is staged locally.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Root cause** — the defect you found, and the evidence in the workspace
   (logs, metrics, code) that connects it to the observed behavior.
2. **Changes** — every file you changed and what you changed in it.
3. **Expected effect** — which metric the fix should move and in which
   direction.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## What the system will run

After you submit the report, the system deletes everything under
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/run`, then re-runs the experiment in your repaired
workspace as a foreground process:

```bash
bash run.sh
```

with this environment:

```text
RLROOT=$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/run
WANDB_MODE=offline
WANDB_DIR=$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/run
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
HF_DATASETS_OFFLINE=1
TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1
```

The effective run uses:

- model `/workspace/models/Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat`
- train and validation data `/workspace/data/gsm8k` (the GSM8K `main` split),
  with the prompt handling and reward logic as shipped
- the budget already in the launch script: `total_train_epochs=3` (87 training
  steps), seed 2, and the allocation plus every other default of
  `examples/math/gsm8k_icepop.yaml` as shipped

`run.sh` launches the full experiment; the held-out evaluation runs at the end
of each of the three epochs. A task-specific grading script then reads **only
this fresh run's** logs under `$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/run` and scores the final
held-out evaluation. Logs written anywhere else are ignored, and so are the
frozen historical logs already staged under `run/` — do not copy, edit, or
fabricate log metrics, and do not replay the frozen historical logs as a new
run. Otherwise the run is scored 0.

The rerun must keep the task's data and code: the GSM8K dataset files, the
model directory's configuration and tokenizer files, the framework source
tree (`areal/`), the example entry points (`examples/`), and the project lock
files are pinned by sha256 at grading time, so changing any of them fails the
run, and a run that does not reach its final held-out evaluation fails the
completeness check.
I’ll inspect the staged configuration, code, and evaluation evidence, then repair any supported defect and write `/workspace/report.md`. I’ll keep all checks local and won’t launch training.

tools.exec_command({cmd:"for p in /AGENTS.md /user/AGENTS.md /user/user1/AGENTS.md /user/user1/harbor-runs/AGENTS.md /user/user1/harbor-runs/d4dd3925def4/AGENTS.md /workspace/AGENTS.md; do if test -f \"$p\"; then cat \"$p\"; fi; done",max_output_tokens:5000}),
tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat run.sh",max_output_tokens:6000}),
tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat examples/math/gsm8k_icepop.yaml",max_output_tokens:8000}),
tools.exec_command({cmd:"rg --files -g 'AGENTS.md' -g '!models/**' -g '!data/**' -g '!run/**'; du -ah run | sort -h | tail -50",max_output_tokens:4000}),
tools.exec_command({cmd:"git status --short; git log -3 --oneline",max_output_tokens:2000})
]);results.forEach((r,i)=>text({i,...r}));

steps.message: The source and token dumps explain why clipping did not prevent the drift: with one minibatch per update, current and proximal log-probabilities match before the optimizer step, so the PPO ratio is 1 and clipping never activates. I’ll lower the peak actor learning rate from `3e-6` to `2e-6` and add cosine decay across all 87 steps to reduce late-run drift.

    argv=shlex.split(command)

        cfg=compose(config_name='gsm8k_icepop',overrides=argv[4:])

def differences(a,b,prefix=''):
    result=[]
    for k in a.keys()|b.keys():
        key=prefix+k
        if k not in a or k not in b:
            result.append((key,a.get(k),b.get(k)))
        elif isinstance(a[k],dict) and isinstance(b[k],dict):

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /workspace/report.md
+# Staged experiment review
+
+**Verdict: unhealthy.** The run completes and improves some final-suite tasks, but its held-out GSM8K performance deteriorates after the first epoch, alongside unstable policy updates and worsening rollout efficiency.
+
+1. **Root cause and evidence**
+
+   The supported diagnosis is excessive cumulative policy drift under an undiminished actor learning rate. The effective historical configuration uses AdamW at a constant `3e-6` for all 87 updates, one PPO minibatch, no reference KL penalty, and token masking at behavior-to-proximal probability-ratio bounds `[0.67, 1.5]`. The warmup fraction `0.001` becomes `int(87 * 0.001) = 0` steps. These settings appear in `run/experiments/logs/user/kt-seeds/icepop_w067-s2/config.yaml` and the original `run.sh`.
+
+   The following values come from parsing the actual per-step tables in that directory's `main.log`. Except for the held-out row, values are means across each epoch's 29 steps.
+
+   | Signal | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 |
+   | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+   | End-of-epoch `eval-rollout/reward` | 0.64481 | 0.54625 | 0.57771 |
+   | Training `ppo_actor/task_reward/avg` | 0.74781 | 0.68322 | 0.64561 |
+   | Total sequence length | 304.0 | 372.5 | 540.2 |
+   | Incorrect sequence length | 378.7 | 580.9 | 949.0 |
+   | `update/entropy/avg` | 0.18454 | 1.38374 | 1.81161 |
+   | `update/rs_filtered_fraction` | 4.10% | 20.48% | 42.80% |
+   | Reported `no_eos_ratios/avg` | 0.394% | 0.677% | 1.310% |
+   | Actor training time per step | 27.91 s | 34.42 s | 50.37 s |
+
+   Held-out results occur at steps 29, 58, and 87 (`main.log:2249`, `:4366`, `:6483`). The final result is 6.71 percentage points below epoch 1. Around steps 33–48, training reward falls from 0.80664 to 0.46387 while entropy rises from 0.21529 to 4.0783. Entropy later oscillates between roughly 0.055 and 5.92. Gradient norms peak at 4.6444, although every logged optimizer update is finite and successful. Weight synchronization remains approximately 2.5–2.8 seconds per step. The run reaches step 87 and reports completion after 5504.49 seconds (`main.log:6497`); there is no training-time OOM, NaN, or traceback in the main or actor log. This supports optimization deterioration rather than a failed launch or stalled synchronization.
+
+   The loss implementation explains why the configured clipping bounds do not constrain that drift. `areal/trainer/rl_trainer.py:782` computes proximal log-probabilities immediately before the update. `areal/trainer/ppo/actor.py:370` uses one minibatch, and `areal/utils/functional/functional.py:585` clips `exp(current_logp - proximal_logp)`. All 36,217 sampled tokens in the twelve frozen `run/ktdump/seeds_icepop_w067_s2/*.parquet` files have exactly equal current and proximal log-probabilities. Accordingly, every logged step has importance ratio 1, approximate proximal KL 0, and clip fraction 0. The subsequent AdamW step can still move the policy; these zeros do not measure its resulting movement or distance from initialization. With `kl_ctl=0`, the trainer also creates no reference model (`rl_trainer.py:203`).
+
+   The same dumps show growing behavior/proximal disagreement before filtering. Across the four rank files at dump calls 0, 1180, and 2340, respectively, 1.81%, 48.39%, and 60.05% of sampled tokens fall outside `[0.67, 1.5]`. At call 2340, mean proximal-minus-behavior log-probability is -5.81, despite the logged near-zero KL on retained tokens. The logging path computes those divergence statistics using the retained-token mask (`actor.py:687`), so it omits much of the disagreement. Rejection is initially modest and becomes severe after instability develops; the evidence does not establish that the unusual mask bounds alone caused the failure.
+
+   Truncation also needs care: `actor.py:333` identifies a sequence as having no EOS by equality with the padded batch width, rather than inspecting EOS or the generation stop reason. Its reported ratio therefore is not a reliable absolute truncation rate. Nevertheless, incorrect sequences lengthen toward the configured 1024-token completion cap, and compute time nearly doubles. Increasing that cap would not address the earlier entropy and held-out deterioration.
+
+   Independent frozen evaluation supports a mixed, unhealthy outcome. `run/eval/final_checkpoint_suite.tsv` reports base → trained accuracy:
+
+   | Benchmark | Base | Trained |
+   | --- | ---: | ---: |
+   | GSM8K | 0.5550 | 0.6073 |
+   | GSM8K exact match | 0.5360 | 0.5967 |
+   | SVAMP | 0.5900 | 0.6367 |
+   | MATH500 | 0.2120 | 0.1360 |
+   | Minerva | 0.0404 | 0.0221 |
+   | Olympiad | 0.0490 | 0.0208 |
+
+   Thus there are real task gains, accompanied by substantial broader regressions. This suite uses a separate evaluation protocol; its GSM8K accuracy should not be substituted for the in-training held-out reward. Training reward alone is insufficient for the verdict.
+
+   Data and reward inspection found no supported alternative cause. The local GSM8K `main` files contain 7473 train and 1319 test examples, no shared question text, no empty questions, and an answer marker in every answer. All training prompt contents fit the 1024-token filter (maximum 221 tokens). `areal/dataset/gsm8k.py` appends the boxed-answer instruction. The actual entry point, `examples/math/gsm8k_rl.py`, runs `MathAgent`, whose reward uses `math_verify.parse/verify` on the completion and answer (`areal/workflow/openai/math_agent.py:21`); it does not use the separate GSM8K reward wrapper. The evaluation path disables reward normalization and evaluates the test split with temperature 0.6. None of these paths was changed.
+
+2. **Changes**
+
+   - `/workspace/run.sh`: reduce `actor.optimizer.lr` from `3e-6` to `2e-6`; override `actor.optimizer.lr_scheduler_type=cosine`; add a comment explaining the observed late-run deterioration. This reduces both the peak step size and continued late-run updates while retaining all 87 steps.
+   - `/workspace/report.md`: add this diagnosis, change inventory, validation results, and expected effects.
+
+   Validation: `bash -n run.sh` passed. Hydra composition of the original and repaired launch arguments confirmed that only those two effective configuration values differ. The seed, three epochs, allocation, generation settings, mask bounds, and epoch evaluation cadence match. A non-training evaluation of the repository's cosine scheduler confirmed finite, decreasing rates: `2e-6` at training step 1, `1.53094e-6` at step 29, `5.31592e-7` at step 58, and `6.51905e-10` at step 87. The sum of learning rates is 33.7% of the original constant schedule; this is an update-budget proxy, not a prediction of parameter displacement. SHA-256 checks confirmed all 528 recorded protected files and frozen evidence files remain unchanged. No training or experiment service was started, and no network was used.
+
+3. **Expected effect**
+
+   The primary expected improvement is higher final fresh-run `eval-rollout/reward` than the historical 0.57771, with a smaller decline after epoch 1. Reduced late-run drift should also lower rejected-token fractions, entropy oscillation, incorrect-response length, and actor compute time. Broader held-out accuracy should retain more of the base model's capability, although that is less directly established by the available evidence.
+
+   The causal diagnosis is an inference from the joint evaluation, rollout, optimization, and token-level evidence. The exact `2e-6` cosine intervention has not been trained or evaluated here; the system's fresh run must establish the resulting accuracy.
*** End Patch"));

Reduced late-run drift should also lower rejected-token fractions, entropy oscillation, incorrect-response length, and actor compute time. Broader held-out accuracy should retain more of the base model's capability, although that is less directly established by the available evidence.
